headline: Bread from air
dek: In 1909 a chemist pulled nitrogen out of the sky and turned it into fertilizer. It worked. Then it kept working.

slides.label: What it was meant to do
slides.title: Fix a coming food shortage
slides.text: Crops need nitrogen. Around 1900 most fertilizer nitrogen came from bird droppings dug off islands near Peru and from saltpeter mined in Chile. Both were running out. In 1898 the chemist William Crookes warned that the world would soon not grow enough wheat.
slides.alt: Workers loading guano into a rail cart at the foot of a huge pale heap, Chincha Islands, Peru, 1865
slides.credit: Guano mining, Chincha Islands, Peru, 1865. Henry de Witt Moulton. Public domain.

slides.label: What went right
slides.title: Half the world eats because of it
slides.text: Fritz Haber found a way to make ammonia from the nitrogen in air. Carl Bosch scaled it up, and the first plant opened in 1913. Roughly half the people alive today eat food grown with it.
slides.alt: A combine harvesting a vast golden wheat field on rolling hills
slides.credit: Wheat harvest on the Palouse. USDA. Public domain.

slides.label: What went oops
slides.title: The extra nitrogen goes somewhere
slides.text: Crops take up only part of it. The rest washes into rivers and the sea, feeds algae and uses up the oxygen. Each summer the Gulf of Mexico grows a dead zone thousands of square miles wide.
slides.alt: Satellite view of brown and green water spreading from the Louisiana coast into the deep blue Gulf of Mexico
slides.credit: Sediment and phytoplankton in the Gulf of Mexico, 2023. NASA. Public domain.
also: Nitrous oxide, a strong greenhouse gas

slides.label: What they got right
slides.title: The chemistry still holds
slides.text: More than a century later the world still makes ammonia the way Haber and Bosch did. The fixes being tried now leave the process alone and use less of it: fertilizer applied at the right time, in the right amount, in the right place.

slides.label: Could anyone have seen it coming?
slides.title: Partly
slides.text: The use in explosives was obvious by 1914. The damage to rivers, coasts and the climate was understood much later, once fertilizer use had grown many times over.

slides.label: Pattern
slides.title: Solve a shortage, create a surplus
